nodes.name: Backward, update and forward unlocking
nodes.statement: Backward \textit{\textbf{un}locking} would permit updates of all modules once forward signals have propagated to all subsequent modules, update \textit{\textbf{un}locking} would permit updates of a module \textit{before} a signal has reached all subsequent modules, and forward \textit{\textbf{un}locking} would permit a module to operate asynchronously from its predecessor and dependent modules.
nodes.statement_short: Backward/update/forward unlocking: a module may update after forward propagation, before the signal reaches upper modules, or run asynchronously.

nodes.name: Decoupled Neural Interfaces (DNI)
nodes.statement: Thus \citet{jaderberg2016decoupled} and \citet{czarnecki2017} propose and analyze Decoupled Neural Interfaces (DNI), a method that uses an auxiliary network to predict the gradient of the backward pass directly from the input.
nodes.origin_citation: Jaderberg et al. 2016; Czarnecki et al. 2017
differentia: uses an auxiliary network to predict the gradient of the backward pass directly from the input

nodes.name: Sample stream S
nodes.statement: We mainly consider the online setting and assume a stream of samples or mini-batches denoted $\mathcal{S}\triangleq\{(x_0^t,y^t)\}_{t\leq T}$, run during $T$ iterations.

nodes.name: DNI auxiliary net
nodes.statement: There, each network module has an associated \textit{auxiliary net} which, given the output activation of the module, predicts the gradient signal from subsequent modules: the module can thus perform an update while modules above are still forward processing.
nodes.statement_short: In DNI each module has an auxiliary net predicting, from its output activation, the gradient from upper modules.

nodes.name: Synchronous DGL (Sync-DGL)
nodes.statement: \small \caption{Synchronous DGL} \SetAlgoLined \DontPrintSemicolon \KwIn{Stream $\mathcal{S}\triangleq\{(x_0^t,y^t)\}_{t\leq T}$ of samples or mini-batches.} \textbf{Initialize} Parameters $\{\theta_j,\gamma_j\}_{j\leq J}$.\; \For { $(x_0^t,y^t) \in \mathcal{S}$ } { \For {$j \in 1,..., J$} {$x^t_j \leftarrow f_{\theta_{j-1}}(x^t_{j-1})$.\; Compute $\nabla_{(\gamma_j,\theta_j)}\hat{ \mathcal{L}}(y^t,x^t_j;\gamma_j,\theta_j)$.\; $(\theta_j,\gamma_j)\leftarrow$Update parameters $(\theta_j,\gamma_j)$. } }
input: Stream $\mathcal{S}\triangleq\{(x_0^t,y^t)\}_{t\leq T}$ of samples or mini-batches.
nodes.statement_short: For each mini-batch, every module j computes its output, the gradient of its local auxiliary loss, and updates its own parameters, so modules update in parallel.
nodes.label: algo:basic

nodes.name: Asynchronous DGL with Replay
nodes.statement: \small \SetAlgoLined \DontPrintSemicolon \KwIn{Stream $\mathcal{S}\triangleq\{(x_0^t,y^t)\}_{t\leq T}$; Distribution of the delay $p=\{p(j)\}_{j}$; Buffer size $M$.} \textbf{Initialize:} Buffers $\{B_j\}_{j}$; params $\{\theta_j,\gamma_j\}_{j}$.\\ \While{\normalfont{\textbf{ training}}}{Sample $j$ in $\{1,...,J\}$ following $p$.\\ \uIf{$j=1$}{ $ (x_{0},y)\gets \mathcal{S}$}\Else{ $(x_{j-1},y)\gets B_{j-1}$.} $x_j \leftarrow f_{\theta_{j-1}}(x_{j-1})$.\; Compute $\nabla_{(\gamma_j,\theta_j)}\hat{ \mathcal{L}}(y,x_j;\gamma_j,\theta_j)$.\; $(\theta_j,\gamma_j)\leftarrow$ Update parameters $(\theta_j,\gamma_j)$.\; \lIf{$j<J$}{ $B_{j} \gets (x^{j},y)$. }} \caption{Asynchronous DGL with Replay}
nodes.statement_short: Repeatedly sample a module j by the delay pmf, read its input from the previous module's replay buffer, take a local gradient step, and write its output to its own buffer.
nodes.label: algo:buffer_sym

nodes.name: Data, labels and module representations
nodes.statement: Let $\bm{X}_0$ and $Y$ be the data and labels, $\bm{X_j}$ be the output representation for module $j$.

nodes.name: Per-module objective function
nodes.statement: We will denote the per-module objective function $\hat{\mathcal{L}}(\bm{X}_{j}, Y;\theta_{j},\gamma_{j})$, where the parameters $\theta_j$ correspond to the module parameter (i.e. $\bm{X}_{j+1} =f_{\theta_{j}}(\bm{X}_{j})$).
nodes.statement_short: $\hat{\mathcal{L}}$ is the per-module objective; $\theta_j$ are module parameters with $X_{j+1}=f_{\theta_j}(X_j)$.

nodes.name: Auxiliary network parameters
nodes.statement: Here $\gamma_j$ represents parameters of a auxiliary networks used to predict the final target and compute the local objective.

nodes.name: Greedy training objective
nodes.statement: The greedy training objective is thus given recursively by defining $P_j$: \begin{equation} \min_{\theta_j,\gamma_j}\hat{\mathcal{L}}(\bm{X}_{j}, Y;\theta_{j},\gamma_{j})\tag{$P_j$} , \end{equation} where $\bm{X}_{j} =f_{\theta_{j-1}^*}(\bm{X}_{j-1})$ and $\theta_{j-1}^*$ is the minimizer of Problem (\(P_{j-1}\)).
nodes.statement_short: Greedy objective: module j minimizes its local loss over $(\theta_j,\gamma_j)$ on the output of the optimally trained previous module.

nodes.name: Per-module greedy problem P_j
nodes.statement: \min_{\theta_j,\gamma_j}\hat{\mathcal{L}}(\bm{X}_{j}, Y;\theta_{j},\gamma_{j})\tag{$P_j$},
nodes.label: eq:dap

nodes.name: Sequential greedy layerwise training
nodes.statement: A natural way to solve the optimization problem for $J$ modules, $(P_J)$, is thus by sequentially solving the problems $\{P_{j}\}_{j\leq J}$ starting with $j=1$. This is the approach taken in e.g. \citet{Marquez,huang2017learning,bengio2007greedy,shallow}.
nodes.origin_citation: Bengio et al. 2007; Belilovsky et al. 2019; Huang et al. 2017; Marquez et al. 2018
nodes.statement_short: Solve the greedy problems $P_1,\dots,P_J$ one after another, each on the converged output of the previous one.

nodes.name: Why Sync-DGL is update unlocked
nodes.statement: Note that at line $5$ the subsequent layer can already begin computing line $4$.
nodes.statement_short: Direct: while module j updates (line 5), the next module can already compute its forward pass (line 4).

nodes.name: Sync-DGL achieves update unlocking
nodes.statement: Therefore, this algorithm achieves update unlocking.

nodes.name: Time-varying input distribution of DGL sub-problems
nodes.statement: Finally we emphasize that unlike the sequential solvers of (e.g. \citet{bengio2007greedy,shallow}) the distribution of inputs to each sub-problem solver changes over time, resulting in a learning dynamic whose properties have never been studied nor contrasted with sequential solvers.
nodes.statement_short: Unlike sequential greedy solvers, DGL's sub-problems see input distributions that change over time.

nodes.name: Replay buffer read/write protocol
nodes.statement: Our minimal distributed setting is as follows. Each worker $j$ has a buffer that it writes to and that worker $j+1$ can read from. The buffer uses a simple read/write protocol. A buffer $B_j$ lets layer $j$ write new samples. When it reaches capacity it overwrites the oldest sample. Layer $j+1$ requests samples from the buffer $B_j$. They are selected by a last-in-first-out (LIFO) rule, with precedence for the least reused samples.
nodes.statement_short: Each module writes to its own capacity-limited buffer (overwriting oldest); the next module reads samples LIFO, preferring least-reused ones.

nodes.name: Delay pmf p(j)
nodes.statement: Alg. \ref{algo:buffer_sym} simulates potential delays in such a setup by the use of a probability mass function (pmf) $p(j)$ over workers, analogous to typical asynchronous settings such as \citep{leblond2017asaga}.

nodes.name: Module parameters Theta and samples Z
nodes.statement: At time step $t$, for simplicity we will denote all parameters of a module (including auxiliary) as $\Theta_j^t\triangleq(\theta_j^t,\gamma_j^t)$, and samples as $Z_j^t\triangleq (X_j^t,Y^t)$, which follow the density $p_j^t(z)$.

nodes.name: Converged density of the previous layer
nodes.statement: Let us fix a depth $j$, such that $j>1$ and consider the converged density of the previous layer, $p^*_{j-1}(z)$.

nodes.name: Distance c to the converged density
nodes.statement: We define the following distance: $c^t_{j-1}\triangleq \int |p_{j-1}^t(z)-p_{j-1}^*(z)|\,dz$.

nodes.name: Loss composition and expected risk
nodes.statement: Denoting $\ell$ the composition of the non-negative loss function and the network, we will study the expected risk $\mathcal{L}(\Theta_{j})\triangleq \mathbb{E}_{p^*_{j-1}}[\ell(Z_{j-1};\Theta_j)]$.
nodes.statement_short: $\ell$ is the loss composed with the network; $\mathcal{L}(\Theta_j)$ is its expectation under the converged input density $p^*_{j-1}$.

nodes.name: L-smoothness
nodes.statement: $\mathcal{L}$ is differentiable and its gradient is $L$-Lipschitz.
nodes.origin_citation: Bottou, Curtis & Nocedal 2018; Huo et al. 2018

nodes.name: SGD scheme with learning rate eta_t
nodes.statement: We consider the SGD scheme with learning rate $\{\eta_t\}_t$: \begin{equation} \hspace{-0.5em}\Theta^{t+1}_{j}=\Theta^t_j-\eta_t \nabla_{\Theta_j} \ell(Z_{j-1}^t;\Theta_j^t), \end{equation}\vspace{-3pt} where \(Z^t_{j-1}\sim p_{j-1}^t\).
nodes.statement_short: Per-module SGD update with step sizes $\eta_t$ on samples drawn from the current (time-varying) input density.

nodes.name: Robbins-Monro conditions
nodes.statement: The step sizes satisfy $\sum_t\eta_t=\infty$ yet $\sum_t\eta_t^2<\infty$.
nodes.origin_citation: Bottou, Curtis & Nocedal 2018; Huo et al. 2018

nodes.name: Finite variance
nodes.statement: There exists $G>0$ such that $\forall t,\Theta_j, \mathbb{E}_{p^t_{j-1}}\big[\Vert\nabla_{\Theta_j}\ell(Z_{j-1};\Theta_j)\Vert^2\big]\leq G$.

nodes.name: Convergence of the previous layer
nodes.statement: We assume that $\sum_{t} c^t_{j-1}<\infty$.

nodes.name: Gradient second-moment bound under the converged density
nodes.statement: Under Assumption 3 and 4, for all $\Theta_j,$ one has $ \mathbb{E}_{p^*_{j-1}}\big[\Vert\nabla_{\Theta_j}\ell(Z_{j-1};\Theta_j)\Vert^2\big]\leq G$.

nodes.name: DGL is faster than feedback-based methods by construction
nodes.statement: We will argue that if we take the assumption that each approach runs for the same number of epochs or iterations and applies the same splits of the network then DGL is by construction faster than the other methods which rely on feedback.
nodes.section: Detailed Discussion of Relative Speed of Competing Methods
assumptions: each approach runs for the same number of epochs or iterations and applies the same splits of the network
conclusions: DGL is by construction faster than the other methods which rely on feedback

nodes.name: Argument that DGL is faster
nodes.statement: The relative speeds of these methods are governed by the following: \begin{enumerate} \item Computation besides forward and backward passes on primary network modules (e.g. auxiliary networks forward and backward passes) \item Communication time of sending activations from one module to the next module \item Communication time of sending feedback to the previous module \item Waiting time for signal to reach final module \end{enumerate} As discussed in the text our auxiliary modules which govern (1) for DGL are negligible thus the overhead of (1) is negligible. DNI will inherently have large auxiliary models as it must predict gradients, thus (1) will be much greater than in DGL. (2) should be of equal speed across all methods given the same implementation and hardware. (3) does not exist for the case of DGL but exists for all other cases. (4) applies only in the case of backward unlocking methods (DDG/FA) and does not exist for DNI or DGL as they are update unlocked. Thus we observe that DGL by construction is faster than the other methods.

abla \ell(z,\Theta_j^t)\Vert^2 |p^t_{j-1}(z)-p^*_{j-1}(z)|\,d z} \sqrt{\int |p^t_{j-1}(z)-p^*_{j-1}(z)|\,d z }\ &= \sqrt{\int \Vert
abla \ell(z,\Theta_j^t)\Vert^2 |p^t_{j-1}(z)-p^*_{j-1}(z)|\,d z} \sqrt{c_{j-1}^t} \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: Cauchy-Schwarz bounds the bias by a weighted moment times $\sqrt{c^t}$

nodes.name: Weighted moment at most 2G
nodes.statement:
Then, observe that:  egin{align} \int \Vert
abla \ell(z,\Theta_j^t)\Vert^2 |p^t_{j-1}(z)-p^*_{j-1}(z)|\,d z &\leq \int \Vert
abla \ell(z,\Theta_j^t)\Vert^2  ig(p^t_{j-1}(z)+p^*_{j-1}(z) ig)\,d z\ &=\mathbb{E}_{p^t_{j-1}}[ \Vert
abla \ell(Z_{j-1},\Theta_j^t)\Vert^2 ]+\mathbb{E}_{p^*_{j-1}}[ \Vert
abla \ell(Z_{j-1},\Theta_j^t)\Vert^2 ]\ &\leq 2G \end{align} The last inequality follows from Lemma 4.1 and Assumption 3.
nodes.statement_short: Bound the weighted second moment by 2G using Lemma 4.1 and Assumption 3

nodes.name: Inner-product deviation
nodes.statement:
Then, using again Cauchy-Schwartz inequality:  egin{align}  igg|\Vert
abla\mathcal{L}(\Theta_j^t)\Vert^2- 
abla\mathcal{L}(\Theta_j^t)^{T}\mathbb{E}_{p_{j-1}^t}[
abla_{\Theta_j} \ell(Z_{j-1}^t;\Theta_j^t)] igg| &= igg|
abla\mathcal{L}(\Theta_j^t)^T ig(
abla\mathcal{L}(\Theta_j^t)-\mathbb{E}_{p_{j-1}^t}[
abla_{\Theta_j} \ell(Z_{j-1}^t;\Theta_j^t)] ig) igg|\ &\leq \Vert 
abla \mathcal{L}(\Theta^t_j)\Vert~\Vert \mathbb{E}_{p_{j-1}^t} ig[
abla_{\Theta_j} \ell(Z_{j-1}^t;\Theta_j^t) ig]-
abla\mathcal{L}(\Theta_j^t)\Vert \ &\leq \Vert 
abla \mathcal{L}(\Theta^t_j)\Vert \sqrt{2Gc^t_{j-1}} \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: Cauchy-Schwarz again bounds the inner-product deviation

nodes.name: Expected deviation
nodes.statement:
Then, taking the expectation leads to  egin{align}  ig|\mathbb{E} igg[\Vert
abla\mathcal{L}(\Theta_j^t)\Vert^2- 
abla\mathcal{L}(\Theta_j^t)^{T}\mathbb{E}_{p_{j-1}^t}[
abla_{\Theta_j} \ell(Z_{j-1}^t;\Theta_j^t)] igg] ig|&\leq \mathbb{E}[ igg|\Vert
abla\mathcal{L}(\Theta_j^t)\Vert^2- 
abla\mathcal{L}(\Theta_j^t)^{T}\mathbb{E}_{p_{j-1}^t}[
abla_{\Theta_j} \ell(Z_{j-1}^t;\Theta_j^t)] igg|]\ &\leq \mathbb{E}[\Vert
abla \mathcal{L}(\Theta^t_j)\Vert] \sqrt{2Gc^t_{j-1}}\ &\leq \sqrt{ \mathbb{E}[\Vert
abla \mathcal{L}(\Theta^t_j)\Vert^2] }\sqrt{2Gc^t_{j-1}}\ \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: Take expectation and apply Jensen to the deviation bound

nodes.name: Gradient norm at most G
nodes.statement:
However, observe that by Lemma 4.1 and Jensen inequality:  egin{align} \Vert 
abla\mathcal{L}(\Theta_j^t)\Vert^2 =\Vert \mathbb{E}_{p^*_j}[
abla_{\Theta_j} \ell(Z,\Theta_j^t)]\Vert^2\leq \mathbb{E}_{p^*_j}[ \Vert 
abla_{\Theta_j} \ell(Z,\Theta_j^t)\Vert^2]\leq G \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: Bound the true gradient norm by G via Jensen

nodes.name: Conclude descent lemma
nodes.statement: Combining this inequality and Assumption 3, we get: \begin{align*} \mathbb{E}[\mathcal{L}(\Theta_j^{t+1})]\leq\mathbb{E}[\mathcal{L}(\Theta_j^{t})]-\eta_t\big(\mathbb{E}[\Vert\nabla\mathcal{L}(\Theta_j^t)\Vert^2]-\sqrt{2}Gc^t_{j-1}\big)+\frac{LG}{2}\eta_t^2\,, \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Combine the bounds to get the descent inequality

nodes.name: Speed components
nodes.statement: The relative speeds of these methods are governed by the following: \begin{enumerate} \item Computation besides forward and backward passes on primary network modules (e.g. auxiliary networks forward and backward passes) \item Communication time of sending activations from one module to the next module \item Communication time of sending feedback to the previous module \item Waiting time for signal to reach final module \end{enumerate}
nodes.section: Detailed Discussion of Relative Speed of Competing Methods
nodes.statement_short: List the four components governing relative speed

nodes.name: Component (1)
nodes.statement: As discussed in the text our auxiliary modules which govern (1) for DGL are negligible thus the overhead of (1) is negligible. DNI will inherently have large auxiliary models as it must predict gradients, thus (1) will be much greater than in DGL.
nodes.section: Detailed Discussion of Relative Speed of Competing Methods
nodes.statement_short: Component (1): auxiliary compute negligible for DGL, large for DNI

nodes.name: Component (2)
nodes.statement: (2) should be of equal speed across all methods given the same implementation and hardware.
nodes.section: Detailed Discussion of Relative Speed of Competing Methods
nodes.statement_short: Component (2): equal across methods

nodes.name: Component (3)
nodes.statement: (3) does not exist for the case of DGL but exists for all other cases.
nodes.section: Detailed Discussion of Relative Speed of Competing Methods
nodes.statement_short: Component (3): absent for DGL

nodes.name: Component (4)
nodes.statement: (4) applies only in the case of backward unlocking methods (DDG/FA) and does not exist for DNI or DGL as they are update unlocked.
nodes.section: Detailed Discussion of Relative Speed of Competing Methods
nodes.statement_short: Component (4): only for backward-unlocking methods

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: Thus we observe that DGL by construction is faster than the other methods.
nodes.section: Detailed Discussion of Relative Speed of Competing Methods
nodes.statement_short: Conclude DGL is fastest
